text: The "Word of the Year" (sometimes capitalized as "Word(s) of the Year" and abbreviated as "WOTY" or "WotY") refers to various annual assessments identifying the most significant word(s) or expression(s) in the public sphere during a specific year. The German tradition of "Wort des Jahres" began in 1971 and has been selected annually by the Society of the German Language, with an additional "Unwort des Jahres" (Most Unpleasant Word of the Year) introduced in 1991 to highlight socially inappropriate terms, such as "Überfremdung." Since 1999, Austria has included its own "Word of the Year," organized by the Society for Austrian German (GSÖD), reflecting the pluricentric nature of German; notable selections include the 52-letter word "Bundespräsidentenstichwahlwiederholungsverschiebung" in 2016 and "Elk Emil" in 2025. Similar word-of-the-year selections have occurred in Liechtenstein since 2002, Switzerland since 2003, and Slovenia since 2016, with the Slovenian Sign Language gesture of the year also announced annually in January. In addition, various German dialects have their own Wort des Jahres selections, including Plattdeutsches Wort des Jahres, Wort des Jahres (Sachsen), and Wort des Jahres (Südtirol). The American Dialect Society's Word of the Year, the oldest English-language version, is announced after the end of the calendar year by a vote of independent linguists and is not tied to commercial interests; since 1990, it has designated one or more words or terms, and also selects words in categories such as "Most Outrageous," "Most Creative," and "Most Likely to Succeed." The Australian National Dictionary Centre has announced a Word of the Year since 2006, chosen by editorial staff based on prominence in the Australian social and cultural landscape, though it is not always an Australian word. The Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, published annually since 2015 by Cambridge University Press & Assessment, is selected based on user data, zeitgeist, and language trends; in 2024, "manifest" was chosen, traditionally meaning "obvious" or "to show clearly," but used in 2024 as a verb meaning "to imagine achieving something you want, in the belief doing so will make it more likely to happen," especially by celebrities on social media. Collins English Dictionary has announced a Word of the Year since 2013, with a shortlist of ten words typically released at the end of the year, though only four were announced in 2014; the selection is made by lexicographers, editorial, marketing, and publicity staff in Glasgow and London, with public input previously allowed; words are not required to be new, and usage statistics and a large corpus are used to support selections, with international relevance often considered, such as "fake news" in 2017. Dictionary.com began selecting a Word of the Year in 2010 with "change" and has done so annually in December, based on search trends and news events. Since 2021, The Economist has published a Word of the Year. The Macquarie Dictionary, which covers Australian English, selects a Word of the Year each year by reviewing new words and definitions added to its online dictionary; a public vote in November determines the People's Choice winner, while the Word of the Year Committee—comprising the Editorial Team, David Astle, and language specialist Tiger Webb—selects the most influential word. Merriam-Webster has published a ten-word list annually since 2003, initially based on website page hits and searches, and since 2006 by an online poll and visitor suggestions. Oxford University Press announces both an Oxford Dictionaries UK Word of the Year and a US Word of the Year (which may be the same), selected by editorial staff and lexicographers, with no guarantee of inclusion in any Oxford dictionary. Since 2004, lexicographer Grant Barrett has published an unranked list of words of the year, usually in The New York Times, and Susie Dent, an English lexicographer working for Oxford University Press, has published a column "A Word a Year" since 2004, selecting one word from each of the past 101 years to reflect contemporary preoccupations; her list is subjective and often mistakenly referred to as the "Oxford Dictionary's Word of the Year." Japan has held an annual "New Word/Trendy Phrase Award" since 1984, sponsored by Jiyu Kokuminsha (and U-CAN since 2004), and has selected a "Kanji of the Year" since 1995, with both reflecting current events and attitudes; for example, in 2011, following the Fukushima disaster, the phrase "the possibility of recriticality is not zero" became the top phrase, and the kanji for "bond" (representing family or friendship) was chosen as the kanji of the year. Word of the Year polls have also been conducted in Denmark (2006–2012 and since 2009 with Sproglaboratoriet and Dansk Sprognævn), Norway (since 2012), Portugal (since 2009), Russia (since 2007), and the Netherlands (since 2007), with Spain selecting a word since 2013 and Ukraine since 2013.
